title: The Middle Elamite Kingdom
subtitle: 1,500–1,100 BC · Chogha Zanbil, the Sack of Babylon, and the Elamite Zenith

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The Igehalkid and Shutrukid dynasties, Chogha Zanbil, and the sack of Babylon

entries.label: The Igehalkid Dynasty
entries.hint: Founded by Igehalki, the dynasty consolidated Elam's highland-lowland dual kingship and cultivated marriage ties with the Kassite dynasty ruling Babylon — a period of relative peace and dynastic intermarriage that laid the economic and political foundation for the far more ambitious building and military programs of Igehalki's successors.
entries.note: Igehalkid royal inscriptions, Susa; Kassite-Elamite marriage evidence in Babylonian and Elamite royal titulature.

entries.label: Untash-Napirisha and Chogha Zanbil
entries.hint: Untash-Napirisha founded an entirely new religious capital, Dur-Untash, built around a massive ziggurat dedicated jointly to Susa's god Inshushinak and the highland god Napirisha — a deliberate architectural statement of religious unification between Elam's lowland and highland halves, married to a Kassite Babylonian princess as part of his dynasty's diplomatic strategy.
entries.note: Untash-Napirisha's foundation inscriptions, Chogha Zanbil; Roman Ghirshman, Chogha Zanbil excavations (1951–62).

entries.label: Shutruk-Nahhunte I — the Sack of Babylon
entries.hint: Shutruk-Nahhunte founded the dynasty that brought Elam to its greatest military power, campaigning repeatedly into Babylonia before his culminating 1158 BC conquest ended the four-century-old Kassite dynasty outright and carried its most celebrated monuments back to Susa as war trophies.
entries.note: Shutruk-Nahhunte's own inscriptions on the captured Hammurabi and Naram-Sin monuments, Louvre.

entries.label: Kutir-Nahhunte and Shilhak-Inshushinak — the Zenith
entries.hint: Kutir-Nahhunte briefly installed his own son on the Babylonian throne after his father's conquest, while his successor Shilhak-Inshushinak — the most prolific royal builder in Elamite history — left inscriptions recording the restoration or construction of well over a hundred temples across the kingdom during Elam's final and greatest flowering before its sudden collapse.
entries.note: Shilhak-Inshushinak's building inscriptions, Susa; the scale of the corpus is itself the primary evidence for his reign's building program.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The fall of Kassite Babylon and Nebuchadnezzar I's revenge

entries.label: The Sack of Babylon and the Fall of the Kassites
entries.hint: Shutruk-Nahhunte's decisive campaign against the last Kassite king, Enlil-nadin-ahi, ended the Kassite dynasty's roughly four-century rule over Babylon outright — the Elamite king carried off the Code of Hammurabi stele and the Victory Stele of Naram-Sin among his trophies, both later excavated at Susa and now among the Louvre's most famous holdings.
entries.note: Elamite chronographic sources on the fall of the Kassite dynasty; the recovered monuments' own find-context at Susa.

entries.label: Kutir-Nahhunte's Client King in Babylon
entries.hint: Following the conquest, Kutir-Nahhunte briefly installed his own son as a client ruler over Babylon — an attempt at direct Elamite political control over Mesopotamia's most prestigious throne that native Babylonian resistance would not tolerate for long.
entries.note: Babylonian King List evidence for the brief Elamite-installed rulers of this interval.

entries.label: Nebuchadnezzar I's Counter-Invasion and the Recovery of Marduk
entries.hint: After an initial failed attempt, the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar I invaded Elam in a punishing midsummer campaign, decisively defeated the Elamite army, and recovered the cult statue of Marduk that had been carried off to Susa decades earlier — reversing Shutruk-Nahhunte's triumph and inaugurating a long period of Elamite political eclipse.
entries.note: The 'Marduk Prophecy' and Nebuchadnezzar I's own inscriptions on the Elamite campaign and Marduk's return.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The dual title of Anshan and Susa, and a king's inscribed record of his own reign

entries.label: 'King of Anshan and Susa'
entries.hint: Middle Elamite kings formally styled themselves 'King of Anshan and Susa,' a dual title asserting rule over both the highland Fars plateau and the lowland Khuzestan capital — a titulature that made Elam's characteristic two-centre political geography an explicit, permanent part of royal legitimacy rather than an informal arrangement.
entries.note: Middle Elamite royal titulature, attested across the Igehalkid and Shutrukid inscription corpus.

entries.label: Shilhak-Inshushinak's Inscribed Record of Rule
entries.hint: Shilhak-Inshushinak's inscriptions systematically catalogue his own building and restoration projects across dozens of named towns and temples — an administrative habit of comprehensive self-documentation that has made his reign, ironically, one of the best-attested in all of Elamite history precisely because of his taste for record-keeping.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The ziggurat of Dur-Untash and the gods of highland and lowland Elam

entries.label: The Ziggurat of Dur-Untash
entries.hint: Untash-Napirisha's ziggurat, dedicated jointly to Inshushinak of Susa and Napirisha of the highlands, survives today as the best-preserved ziggurat anywhere in the ancient Near East — its dual dedication a deliberate religious statement binding Elam's lowland and highland cults into a single, shared sacred architecture.
entries.note: Chogha Zanbil excavations, Roman Ghirshman (1951–62); UNESCO World Heritage inscription (1979).

entries.label: The Sit Shamshi Ritual Model
entries.hint: A bronze model depicting two nude figures performing a ritual before a sunrise, inscribed with Shilhak-Inshushinak's own dedication, offers a uniquely concrete visual record of an actual Elamite religious ceremony — rare physical evidence of ritual practice rather than only textual reference to a god's name.
